papers.title: Semantically Rich, Metrically Affect-Blind: A Geometric Blind Spot in Modern Text Embedders
papers.abstract: We report a systematic dissociation in modern text embedders: sentiment is almost perfectly decodable from their embeddings, yet almost entirely absent from their metric. Across eleven frozen encoders spanning 2021 to 2026, including 2026-generation models and the 4B-parameter LLM embedder Qwen3-Embedding-4B, a linear probe recovers sentence polarity at up to 91.3% accuracy while cosine similarity separates polarity by a margin of only 0.003-0.064. Qwen3-Embedding-4B, the strongest probe in the panel, reaches 91.3% probe accuracy but only 64.3 retrieval MAP. Because retrieval, clustering, deduplication, and retrieval-augmented generation operate on the metric rather than on a trained probe, these systems are effectively blind to information their encoder demonstrably contains. A task-conditioning control suggests this reflects the pretraining objective rather than a prompting artifact: conditioning Jina-v5 on its classification task rather than its retrieval task recovers only about half of the MAP gain that injection achieves on the same weights (63.2 to 73.8, versus 85.1), and leaves the alignment gap essentially unchanged. Sentiment-Injected Sentence Embeddings (SISE) train a small (0.13M-0.69M-parameter) supervised-contrastive head on a frozen encoder in seconds on a CPU, using the labelled training set. The head improves every encoder released since 2022 on full-data probe accuracy (up to +5.8 points), retrieval MAP (up to +26.0) and polarity margin (7-61x). This is a specialization, not a free gain: the compact 128-d head loses 38-41 Spearman points on STS-B, while a fused variant that concatenates it with the base embedding loses 2.4-12.0. With the head, a 0.6B encoder at 128 dimensions matches a 4B encoder given the same head (91.8 vs. 90.3 MAP). We release a CPU-reproducible pipeline and a reusable diagnostic, the Attribute Alignment Gap.

deep_reading.content:
Search a vector index for "what do users dislike about this product" and the reviews you get back are usually on topic but a mix of praise and complaints. This paper measures why: across 11 text embedding models, from the 2021 MiniLM to 2026 releases, sentiment is present in the vectors and a simple linear classifier reads it with up to 91.3% accuracy, yet the cosine similarity that retrieval actually uses barely registers it, with the average similarity of same-polarity pairs exceeding opposite-polarity pairs by only 0.003 to 0.064. A small projection head of under 700,000 parameters on top of the frozen embedder, trained in seconds on a CPU, repairs this: ==sentiment-retrieval MAP (mean average precision; higher means same-polarity results rank higher) rises by up to 26 points, at a cost to general semantic similarity that drops to 2.4 to 12 points when the original vector is concatenated==.

My take: teams doing review search, support-ticket search, opinion monitoring, or RAG that must retrieve by attitude should read this. The lesson is practical: a high leaderboard score does not mean the similarity separates the attribute you care about, and a bigger model will not fix it. The repair is cheap and needs no corpus re-encoding. But the experiments use only two English movie-review datasets, the head needs a few thousand labels, and there is no comparison with simpler linear projections.

## What problem does it solve?

Retrieval, clustering, deduplication, recommendation and RAG all reduce to nearest-neighbor search in a vector space. What matters is not whether a vector contains some information but whether similarity changes because of it.

For topic and meaning the two usually coincide. The author finds sentiment is an exception, and measures the two separately:

- Linear probe accuracy: train a logistic-regression classifier on frozen vectors to tell positive from negative. High accuracy means sentiment is in the vector and linearly readable.
- Attribute Alignment Gap (AAG, proposed here): average cosine similarity of same-polarity pairs minus that of opposite-polarity pairs. Near zero means similarity is blind to sentiment.

AAG needs only class labels, no human similarity ratings, takes a few lines of code, and works for any attribute and any embedder.

## Key finding: the information is there, but similarity ignores it

The paper tests 11 frozen embedders from about 22 million to 4 billion parameters, including E5, BGE, mxbai, Snowflake Arctic, Qwen3-Embedding 0.6B and 4B, Microsoft Harrier and Jina-v5, on two English sentiment datasets: SST-2 (movie review sentences) and MR (Rotten Tomatoes reviews).

Results are consistent across all models. On SST-2, probe accuracy rises from 77.4% for MiniLM to 91.3% for Qwen3-4B, clear progress over five years; AAG stays near zero, between 0.003 and 0.064, with no upward trend by year or size. Sentiment-retrieval MAP follows AAG, not probe accuracy.

The starkest case is Qwen3-Embedding-4B: the highest probe accuracy of all, yet retrieval MAP of only 64.3. A bigger model improved semantics without making similarity pay attention to sentiment.

![Figure 1 from the paper: the horizontal axis is linear-probe accuracy (can sentiment be read out), the vertical axis sentiment-retrieval MAP (does similarity use it); SST-2 on the left, MR on the right. The dotted line marks similarity expressing sentiment as well as the probe reads it. Hollow points are original embedders, all far below the line; arrows lead to their position with the repair head (filled points), most moving far up. Color shows release year.](figs/2610.32122/fig_quadrant.png)

## Why this happens

The quantitative explanation is that the sentiment direction holds too small a share of the space. Take the direction between the mean positive and mean negative vectors and measure what fraction of total variance lies along it. On SST-2 it is 2.4% for MiniLM, 4.3% for Qwen3-4B and 6.7% for E5-large. Cosine similarity sums over all dimensions, so a direction holding 4% of the variance barely moves it. The 4B model's share is even lower than the 0.6B Harrier's, so scale does not help.

As for why the share is so small, the author points to the pretraining objective. Contrastive positive pairs are mostly topically related, such as queries and documents or titles and bodies. "This film is superb" and "this film is dreadful" share syntax, topic and entities and differ in one evaluative word, making them near-perfect positives, so training actively compresses the sentiment direction.

A control uses Jina-v5. This model requires the caller to specify a task, such as retrieval or classification, and the same weights produce different vectors for each. That allows a test without changing models: if encoded for classification, does it recover sentiment by itself? Switching to classification raises SST-2 sentiment-retrieval MAP from 63.2 to 73.8, but adding the repair head in retrieval mode reaches 85.1. Switching tasks recovers only about half of the head's gain, and AAG barely moves (0.039 to 0.043). The problem is not just using the wrong mode.

![Figure 2 from the paper: left, the control on identical Jina-v5-small weights, blue for SST-2 and red for MR, showing sentiment-retrieval MAP in retrieval mode, classification mode and retrieval mode with the repair head; classification mode recovers only part of the gap. Right, labels needed by a classifier on SST-2: Harrier-0.6B with the repair head (red) peaks with 2 labels per class, while the original vectors (blue) need 50 to 100; gray is a classic weighted-average GloVe baseline.](figs/2610.32122/fig_control.png)

Sentiment is not the only case. Testing 3 models on 8 more attributes, including news topic, subjectivity, emotion, irony and stance, probes read all of them, for example 62.9 points above the majority baseline for topic, yet AAG never exceeds 0.08 and is mostly below 0.05, against 0.4 to 0.5 in a repaired sentiment space. Even topic, which contrastive learning is meant to capture, has an AAG of only 0.02 to 0.08, so this is a general property of embedders.

## The repair: a small projection head

The method is called SISE (sentiment-injected sentence embeddings). The embedder stays frozen; the training set is encoded once, and a two-layer network (256 hidden units, 128 outputs) is trained on the vectors with supervised contrastive learning: sentences with the same label are pulled together and different labels pushed apart. It has 130,000 to 690,000 parameters depending on input dimension and trains in seconds on a 2-core CPU with 4,000 labeled sentences.

The author stresses this repairs similarity rather than adding information. The probe already shows sentiment is in the vector; the head discards directions that dominate cosine similarity but are irrelevant to sentiment, and amplifies the sentiment direction until it decides what is close. After repair the sentiment direction holds 85.5% to 96.7% of the variance.

## Results

| Embedder | Original probe accuracy | Original MAP | MAP with head | AAG change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| E5-large | 89.7 | 72.2 | 90.1 | 0.023 to 0.409 |
| Arctic-large | 82.2 | 54.4 | 79.6 | 0.005 to 0.264 |
| Qwen3-4B | 91.3 | 64.3 | 90.3 | 0.029 to 0.393 |
| Harrier-0.6B | 90.8 | 73.6 | 91.8 | 0.034 to 0.512 |

The table shows SST-2. The head raises AAG 7 to 61 times and sentiment-retrieval MAP by 9.8 to 26.0 points; every model from 2022 on also gains 1.4 to 5.8 points of full-data probe accuracy, with only the 2021 MiniLM slipping. Across 5 random seeds the standard deviation on SST-2 is at most 1 point, so results are stable, and they are insensitive to output size and temperature.

A useful deployment finding: with the same head, the 0.6B Harrier reaches 91.8 MAP and the 4B Qwen3 90.3, so for sentiment retrieval model size matters far less than the similarity itself. The head's output is only 128 dimensions, 20 times smaller than Qwen3-4B's 2560, and needs no corpus re-encoding, just one extra step on existing vectors.

The cost is measured too. On the general semantic similarity benchmark STS-B (the metric is the rank correlation between model similarity and human similarity ratings, times 100, from 0 to 100), the original vectors score 82 to 88 while the 128-dimensional head scores only 42 to 47, a loss of 38 to 41 points, because it learns only sentiment and drops everything else. Concatenating the original vector with the head output cuts the loss to 2.4 to 12 points. The head alone suits a dedicated sentiment index; use the concatenated version when one index must serve both.

## Limitations as I see them

First, the data is narrow. Repair experiments use only two English binary movie-review datasets with 4,000 training examples each, and 8B to 12B embedders are untested.

Second, simpler baselines are missing. The author acknowledges no comparison with linear discriminant analysis or rescaling along the probe direction, with SentiCSE (a dedicated sentiment sentence encoder), or with giving the embedder a sentiment instruction. These may capture much of the gain.

Third, read the few-shot result carefully. "Two labels per class reaches the ceiling" in Figure 2 assumes the head was trained on 4,000 labels; it is not true few-shot learning.

Fourth, AAG is an absolute cosine difference, and similarity distributions differ between models, so comparing AAG values across models is not strict; read it alongside retrieval MAP.

## How a team could try it

1. Diagnose first: label a few hundred examples of your data for the attribute you care about (sentiment, urgency, complaint or not) and compute AAG and probe accuracy. High probe accuracy with AAG near zero means you have the same problem.
2. Then repair: train a small projection head on a few thousand labels with the public code, which runs on a CPU.
3. For deployment, choose between a dedicated 128-dimensional index and concatenating the head output to the original vector; the latter affects general retrieval less.
4. Before launch, compare with a linear approach such as amplifying the probe direction to confirm the nonlinear head is needed.

## Bottom line

==Embedders contain sentiment but cosine similarity barely uses it, and bigger models do not fix that; measure AAG first, then a small head trained in seconds lets retrieval separate results by attitude.==

| Dimension | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Problem importance | High. Review, ticket and opinion search all rely on similarity separating attitude |
| Novelty | Medium. The diagnostic and causal analysis are clear; the head is standard supervised contrastive learning |
| Evidence | Medium. 11 models and 9 attributes, but repair is tested on two English datasets without simple linear baselines |
| Engineering cost | Very low. Seconds on a CPU, no re-encoding, public code |
| Worth trying | Teams that retrieve by attribute should compute AAG once |

papers.title: What the Query Remembers: Query Abstraction Governs Lexical and Dense Retrieval of Classical Arabic Poetry
papers.authors: Omar Farouk Zouak, Selma Mani, Larbi Said Chikh, Raid Abderrezak Ouahioune
papers.abstract: How well a poetry archive can be searched depends on what the user still remembers, not only on what the model understands. We show this for Classical Arabic poetry, benchmarking nine dense encoders and BM25 over two corpora, three indexing modes and two evaluation protocols. Which retriever wins is governed by how much of a poem's wording the query still carries. On tip-of-the-tongue queries BM25 leads every dense encoder, including an 8B state-of-the-art model (0.746 vs. 0.717 Recall@5); on abstract queries it falls to eighth out of ten (0.392 vs. 0.748). Editing the wording of the same queries shows that this ranking largely reflects query composition: adding one remembered half-verse raises BM25 by 38 points, rewriting the quoted words by hand leaves BM25 level with the 8B encoder, and BM25's sensitivity to remembered wording is significantly steeper than that of the strongest dense encoder. The same axis controls explanation augmentation, whose effect swings from +37 to -39 points. The mechanism splits by system type: lexical containment predicts BM25's behaviour, while embedding proximity predicts dense encoders. Finally, the field's two standard protocols, known-item retrieval and thematic relevance, dissociate on the same systems, a result reproduced by two blind human annotators and by two open-weights judges, one of them under a rubric with no literal-match criterion. A benchmark that reports one protocol, or one query register, can give a materially wrong picture. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ellzo/what-the-query-remembers.

deep_reading.title: What the Query Remembers: Query Abstraction Governs Lexical and Dense Retrieval of Classical Arabic Poetry
deep_reading.content:
When searching a classical Arabic poetry archive, which works better: keyword search with BM25 or an embedding model? This paper finds that the answer depends mainly on how much of the original wording the user still remembers. When users half-remember a few lines, BM25 beats all nine embedding models, including the 8-billion-parameter Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Recall@5 of 0.746 versus 0.717). When users can only describe what the poem is about, BM25 drops to 8th of 10 systems (0.392 versus 0.748). By rewriting the same queries, the authors show that the ranking is driven mainly by whether the query contains original wording. ==Adding half a verse of the original to a query raises BM25 recall by 37.8 points; adding a BM25 arm to fused retrieval gains 6.1 points on the half-remembered query set but loses 9.7 points on the theme-only query set==.

My take: this is worth reading for any team building content search, not just teams working on Arabic or poetry. The conclusion transfers directly. The same retrieval system can have opposite best configurations for different kinds of queries, so before choosing a design you need to know whether your users' queries carry original wording. The experimental design is also worth copying. Instead of only comparing two datasets, the authors rewrite the same queries to test cause and effect. The limits are that the corpus is only classical Arabic poetry, the queries were written by the authors, and there are only about 500 known-item queries.

## What problem is it actually solving?

Classical Arabic poetry is hostile to retrieval. Arabic words change form heavily around their roots, vowel marks are usually omitted in writing, and poems are full of wordplay and metaphor, so the literal wording is far from the meaning. That makes it a common stress test for whether embedding models retrieve by meaning rather than by surface form.

The authors started with a simple question: how well do current embedding models retrieve classical Arabic poetry? They found the question has no single answer. Users remember different things. Some remember half a line, and some remember only what the poem was about. Where a query sits on this abstraction scale decides which retriever wins, by how much, and whether common improvements help or hurt.

## How the experiments are set up

The authors use two corpora. Each poem is split into overlapping three-line chunks that are encoded separately, and a poem's score is the maximum of its chunk scores.

- Fann or Flop: 4,687 poems with human-written explanations of the verses. Its 244 queries simulate a user who half-remembers the poem. The query writers had seen the poem and could freely include remembered wording, and 32.8% of queries share an exact three-word run with the target poem.
- Diwan: to keep computation manageable, 3,500 poems were sampled from a 14-million-line corpus, 70 each from the 50 most frequent poets. Its 258 queries are deliberately written as abstract descriptions of content, and only 2.7% contain original wording.

For example, one half-remembered query is "a satirical poem about an ugly lover that opens: say much or say little, we are tired of you". One abstract query is "a philosophical poem that denies reincarnation and urges trust in reason alone", which shares no words with the poem.

The contestants are nine embedding models (including Qwen3-Embedding 0.6B and 8B, BGE-M3, multilingual E5 and jina-v3) plus BM25. There are three index types: the original verses, plain-language explanations generated by Gemini in place of the verses, and the human explanations that come with Fann or Flop. The main metric is Recall@5, the share of queries whose target poem appears in the top five results.

## Finding one: the winner depends on the query

On Fann or Flop, BM25 ranks first and edges out Qwen3-8B (0.746 versus 0.717, not significant). On Diwan, BM25 falls to 8th and Qwen3-8B leads by 36 points. Scaling the same model family from 0.6B to 8B gains 17 and 22 points on the two corpora, but the 8B model still does not pass BM25 on Fann or Flop. Model size alone does not close this gap.

However, the corpus and the query style change together, so this comparison alone cannot say which factor matters. The authors therefore run two checks inside the same corpus.

The first check is stratification. The 244 Fann or Flop queries are split by whether they share an exact three-word run with the target poem: 80 quote it and 164 do not. BM25 finds every target in the quoting group (Recall@5 of 1.000) and drops to 0.622 in the non-quoting group. On non-quoting queries, BM25 and Qwen3-8B are no longer significantly different (0.622 versus 0.646). So BM25's overall lead comes entirely from the quoting queries.

The second check rewrites the same queries while keeping the information need and target poem fixed:

| Rewrite | BM25 recall change | Qwen3-8B recall change |
|---|---:|---:|
| Add the opening half-verse to non-quoting queries | up 37.8 points | up 23.2 points |
| Add a middle half-verse | up 37.8 points | up 20.7 points |
| Add the final half-verse | up 37.8 points | up 12.8 points |
| Rewrite the quote out of quoting queries by hand | down 35.4 points | down 19.0 points |

The table shows that BM25 gains the most when wording is added and loses the most when it is removed, and its difference from Qwen3-8B is significant in both directions. The embedding model is affected too, just less. Once the quote is removed, BM25 and Qwen3-8B tie, just as in the naturally non-quoting group. A regression controlling for query length, proper nouns and poem length leaves the overlap effect essentially unchanged.

## Finding two: the same fix can help or hurt

Since the verses are hard to understand, a natural idea is to index plain-language explanations instead. Whether that helps depends entirely on the query type.

On Diwan, with abstract queries, replacing verses with AI explanations improves all ten systems, and BM25 rises from 0.392 to 0.760, a gain of 37 points. On Fann or Flop, with half-remembered queries, the same replacement hurts most systems, and BM25 falls from 0.746 to 0.357, a loss of 39 points, because the remembered wording no longer appears in the explanation.

papers.title: PersonalQuery-Benchmark:Evaluating Retrieval Robustness to Personalized User Expression Differences
papers.authors: Wenyu Liang, Hongzhi Yin, Tongtong Wu, Fan Liu, Kexin Dai, Weiqing Wang
papers.abstract: Existing personalized information retrieval methods mainly model differences in user needs through user preferences and query intent, while paying little attention to the personalized expression differences that arise when different users express the same retrieval need. Existing real query data typically lack stable user identities, long-term expression histories, and intent-matched counterparts, making it difficult to systematically evaluate the impact of personalized expression differences on retrieval outcomes. To this end, we propose PersonalQuery-Benchmark (PQB). PQB models personalized syntactic expression and personalized writing errors from users' historical texts, constructs personalized syntactic expression queries and personalized writing-error queries, and validates benchmark quality through LLM assessment and independent human evaluation. PQB covers three Amazon product domains with 6,516 query instances in total, and is evaluated on five retrieval models representing lexical, learned sparse, dense bi-encoder, late-interaction, and hybrid architectures, together with two LLM-based ranking models. Results show that even when the information need is held fixed, personalized expression differences still induce measurable ranking variation; different retrieval models exhibit clearly different sensitivities to syntactic variation and writing-error variation, while higher overall retrieval effectiveness does not necessarily correspond to stronger robustness against expression variation. PQB provides a new benchmark and evaluation framework for systematically studying personalized expression robustness. The associated code and dataset are available at the following address: https://github.com/cpxjazz123/PersonalQuery-Benchmark.
papers.summary: Two shoppers want the same product. One asks for strawberry, lactose-free Greek yogurt in a short phrase; the other writes a longer sentence and misspells a word along the way. Will search return the same results? This paper builds a benchmark, PQB, from real user reviews in three Amazon categories to test whether results hold up when the same need is worded differently. They often do not. With the core product terms identical and only sentence structure changed, among query pairs where one query puts the target product first, roughly 27% to 52% of the time the other does not. Misspellings that follow the user's own typing habits cut the top-20 hit rate by up to 12.3 percentage points. ==Models with better overall effectiveness are not necessarily more robust==.

deep_reading.content:
Two shoppers want the same product. One types "I want strawberry, lactose-free Greek yogurt", and the other types "I am looking for a Greek yogurt which is strawberry flavored and lactose-free" and misspells a word along the way. Will search return the same results? This paper builds a benchmark, PQB, from real user reviews in three Amazon categories to test exactly this kind of "same need, different wording". The answer is no, and the gap is sizable. With the five core product terms held identical and only the sentence structure changed, among query pairs where at least one query puts the target product at rank 1, roughly 27% to 52% of the time the other query does not, across seven retrieval setups. ==Adding misspellings that follow the user's own typing habits cuts the top-20 hit rate by up to 12.3 percentage points (BM25), while the BGE-M3 hybrid retriever loses the least, only 4.9 points; models with better overall effectiveness are not necessarily more robust==.

My take: teams running e-commerce or question-answering search can borrow this evaluation idea to check, before launch, how sensitive their system is to differences in how users phrase things. The most useful finding is that "effective is not the same as robust". The two large-language-model rerankers have the best hit rates, yet misspellings hurt them about as much as BM25, because they only rerank BM25's top 25 candidates. The weakness is that every query is generated by a small 0.5-billion-parameter model and then selected, not written by real users. The "personalized" part mainly lives in how queries are selected and how errors are added, and the retrieval evaluation has no random-rewrite control to show how much that personalization matters.

## What problem is it actually solving?

Personalized retrieval usually focuses on what users want: preferences, past behavior and intent. This paper looks at the other side, which is how users say it. For the same need, some people list attributes in short phrases and others write full clauses. Some never make typos and others keep swapping adjacent letters. These differences have nothing to do with the need itself, but they affect retrieval.

The difficulty is the lack of evaluation data. Real query logs rarely carry stable user identities and long writing histories, and it is hard to find query pairs with exactly the same need but different wording. PQB sets out to construct such pairs, with each query worded as much as possible like a specific real user.

![Figure 1: two ways to express the same yogurt need. The top sentence is a simple list of attributes; the bottom one opens with "I am looking for", uses a relative clause, and misspells lactose-free as lacseto-free (two letters swapped). Both contain the brand, flavor, lactose-free attribute and price.](figs/2610.32164/figure1.png)

## How the benchmark is built

The data comes from Amazon Reviews 2023, using three categories: musical instruments, video games and baby products. A product a user has reviewed becomes a retrieval target, and the product's title, description and features are concatenated into the document being searched.

Step one builds a syntactic profile for each user. The authors extract structural rules from the user's past reviews, such as dependency relations like "noun modified by adjective" and runs of three part-of-speech tags. Each review sentence becomes a sparse vector of about 22,000 dimensions. An encoder is then trained to compress it to 16 dimensions, pulling sentences from the same user together and pushing different users apart. Finally, a Gaussian distribution is fitted to each user's 16-dimensional sentence vectors as that user's syntactic habit.

Step two generates candidate queries. Five core retrieval terms are fixed for each product, and Qwen2.5-0.5B generates many first-person shopping queries. Each query must contain each of the five terms exactly once and may not add new attributes. Only function words, modifiers and clause structure may change. Among the retained queries for a product, every pair must have a cosine similarity of at least 0.9 under the all-mpnet-base-v2 sentence encoder, which keeps the meaning nearly identical.

Step three picks one query for each of two users. For a given product, a candidate query "belongs" to user A when three conditions hold. Its Mahalanobis distance to A's Gaussian center falls inside the 95% acceptance region (the 95th percentile of a 16-dimensional chi-square distribution, 26.3). It falls outside B's acceptance region. Its log density under A's distribution is at least 1 higher than under B's. Among user pairs where both users have eligible queries, the authors pick the pair whose Gaussians differ the most, measured by the Bhattacharyya distance, which accounts for both the centers and the covariances. Each user then gets the eligible query with the highest density under their own distribution. Every product thus ends up with two queries of the same content but clearly different wording.

Step four adds misspellings. A grammar-correction tool first fixes the user's past reviews, and comparing the original with the corrected text reveals which kinds of errors this user tends to make, such as swapped letters, doubled letters or adjacent-key slips. The user's query is then rewritten. Only words of three or more letters are changed, words where this user's historical character error rate is higher come first, and at most three distinct words per query are changed. For each chosen word, the method first looks in the user's own error history for a character edit it can copy, preferring one whose misspelled word had the same dependency relation and part of speech as the current word. For example, if the user once swapped two letters in the same syntactic position, the current word gets its letters swapped too. If nothing can be reused, an error type is drawn according to how often the user makes each kind. The edited query must still have a sentence-vector similarity of at least 0.9 with the original, or it is discarded.

![Figure 2: the construction pipeline. The top row learns syntactic Gaussians from user review histories; the middle row generates candidate queries from product metadata, selects personalized syntactic queries, and adds misspellings by the user's error habits to form clean and misspelled query pairs; the bottom row is quality validation and retrieval evaluation.](figs/2610.32164/figure2.png)

The final benchmark has 6,516 queries: 3,654 personalized syntactic queries plus 2,862 successfully generated misspelled versions of them.

On quality, human raters scored naturalness at 4.21 out of 5. In another test, annotators first saw a user's past reviews. They were then shown two queries with the same product and core attributes but different sentence structure, one selected using this user's syntactic profile and one a control, in random order. Annotators had to say which one read more like this user. They picked the personalized query 66.3% of the time against a 50% chance level, which means the selected queries do carry recognizable personal syntax.

## Result one: changing only sentence structure changes hits

The authors test seven retrieval setups: BM25, SPLADE (learned sparse retrieval), GTE-base (dense vectors), ColBERTv2 (token-level interaction), BGE-M3 hybrid retrieval, and Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-Reranker-8B reranking BM25's top 25 results.

The main metric is the flip rate. Among query pairs where at least one query hits the top K, it is the share where only one of the two hits. A flip rate of 40% means that whenever one user sees the target product at rank 1, the other user has a 40% chance of not seeing it there.

| Retrieval setup | Flip rate at rank 1 | Flip rate in top 10 | Top-20 hit-rate drop from misspellings |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| BM25 | 41.7% | 27.8% | 12.3 points |
| SPLADE | 26.6% | 12.5% | 5.9 points |
| GTE-base | 40.4% | 24.1% | 6.2 points |
| ColBERTv2 | 52.2% | 36.4% | 7.1 points |
| BGE-M3 hybrid | 36.3% | 19.2% | 4.9 points |
| Llama-3.1-8B reranking | 42.0% | 27.8% | 12.0 points |
| Qwen3-Reranker-8B reranking | 43.3% | 24.9% | 11.4 points |

The table shows averages over the three categories. Every setup has a nonzero flip rate, which shows that sentence structure alone can change results. SPLADE is the most stable and ColBERTv2 the least. ColBERTv2 compares every query token against every document token, so function words and clause structure also enter the score. That may be why it is the most sensitive to phrasing, though the paper does not test this directly. Flip rates also do not fall steadily as K grows, so a single cutoff is not enough to judge stability.

## Result two: users' own misspellings consistently hurt

The effect of misspellings runs one way. All seven setups lose hit rate and mean reciprocal rank at every cutoff. BM25 drops the most, because a single wrong letter means the word no longer matches at all. BGE-M3 hybrid combines dense vectors, sparse weights and token-level interaction, and it drops the least.

The two large-language-model rerankers deserve attention. On clean queries they have the highest hit rates of all seven setups. In baby products, for instance, both reach a 38.4% top-5 hit rate, against 32.2% for BM25 and only 16.1% for GTE-base. Yet misspellings hurt them almost as much as BM25. The reason is in the configuration: they only rerank BM25's top 25 candidates, so once a typo keeps BM25 from retrieving the target, no reranker can see it. The drop at top 20 is also generally larger than at rank 1, which means typos do damage beyond the very top of the ranking.

## Limitations as I see them

First, the queries are not written by real users. Every candidate is generated by Qwen2.5-0.5B under strict constraints and then selected by user profile. Real users may vary more, for example by dropping core terms or adding irrelevant details, and PQB forbids both.

Second, there is no random-rewrite control. The paper verifies that personalized misspellings resemble the target user more than global or random errors do, but the retrieval evaluation does not compare rewrites that follow user habits with random rewrites. So how much "personalization" adds to the retrieval conclusions remains unclear.

Third, the evaluation is small and absolute hit rates are low. Baby products has only about 400 queries, and in that category even the best setup reaches only about 53% top-20 hit rate. Flip rates are computed only over pairs where at least one query hits, so the denominator differs by setup and cross-setup comparisons need care.

## How a team could try this

1. Find different queries in your production logs that led to clicks on the same product, group them by sentence form and whether they contain typos, and compute a similar flip rate to see how sensitive your live system is.
2. If you use BM25 retrieval followed by a large-model reranker, evaluate recall on misspelled queries separately, and consider adding dense retrieval or spelling correction at the retrieval stage rather than relying on reranking.
3. When comparing retrieval designs, report a stability metric alongside average hit rate, such as result agreement across different phrasings of the same need.
4. PQB's code and data are public, so you can run an offline evaluation on its three categories directly.

## One-sentence conclusion

==Rephrasing the same need or adding a user's habitual typos changes retrieval results noticeably; hybrid retrieval copes best with typos, while the most effective large-model rerankers are not more robust because they are bounded by BM25 recall.==

| Dimension | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Importance | Medium-high. E-commerce and question-answering search both face differences in user phrasing |
| Novelty | Medium. Building query pairs from syntactic Gaussian profiles and personal error habits is carefully designed |
| Evidence | Medium. Seven setups, three categories and human validation, but the queries are generated and there is no random-rewrite control |
| Engineering cost | Low. Code and data are public for offline evaluation |
| Worth trying | Yes, borrow the flip-rate metric to check your own retrieval system |

Each user then gets the eligible query with the highest density under their own distribution. Every product thus ends up with two queries of the same content but clearly different wording.

Step four adds misspellings. A grammar-correction tool first fixes the user's past reviews, and comparing the original with the corrected text reveals which kinds of errors this user tends to make, such as swapped letters, doubled letters or adjacent-key slips. The user's query is then rewritten. Only words of three or more letters are changed, words where this user's historical character error rate is higher come first, and at most three distinct words per query are changed. For each chosen word, the method first looks in the user's own error history for a character edit it can copy, preferring one whose misspelled word had the same dependency relation and part of speech as the current word. For example, if the user once swapped two letters in the same syntactic position, the current word gets its letters swapped too. If nothing can be reused, an error type is drawn according to how often the user makes each kind. The edited query must still have a sentence-vector similarity of at least 0.9 with the original, or it is discarded.

The final benchmark has 6,516 queries: 3,654 personalized syntactic queries plus 2,862 successfully generated misspelled versions of them.

On quality, human raters scored naturalness at 4.21 out of 5. In another test, annotators first saw a user's past reviews. They were then shown two queries with the same product and core attributes but different sentence structure, one selected using this user's syntactic profile and one a control, in random order. Annotators had to say which one read more like this user. They picked the personalized query 66.3% of the time against a 50% chance level, which means the selected queries do carry recognizable personal syntax.

Result one: changing only sentence structure changes hits

The authors test seven retrieval setups: BM25, SPLADE (learned sparse retrieval), GTE-base (dense vectors), ColBERTv2 (token-level interaction), BGE-M3 hybrid retrieval, and Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-Reranker-8B reranking BM25's top 25 results.

The main metric is the flip rate. Among query pairs where at least one query hits the top K, it is the share where only one of the two hits. A flip rate of 40% means that whenever one user sees the target product at rank 1, the other user has a 40% chance of not seeing it there.

GTE-base40.4%24.1%6.2 points

The table shows averages over the three categories. Every setup has a nonzero flip rate, which shows that sentence structure alone can change results. SPLADE is the most stable and ColBERTv2 the least. ColBERTv2 compares every query token against every document token, so function words and clause structure also enter the score. That may be why it is the most sensitive to phrasing, though the paper does not test this directly. Flip rates also do not fall steadily as K grows, so a single cutoff is not enough to judge stability.

Result two: users' own misspellings consistently hurt

The effect of misspellings runs one way. All seven setups lose hit rate and mean reciprocal rank at every cutoff. BM25 drops the most, because a single wrong letter means the word no longer matches at all. BGE-M3 hybrid combines dense vectors, sparse weights and token-level interaction, and it drops the least.

The two large-language-model rerankers deserve attention. On clean queries they have the highest hit rates of all seven setups. The reason is in the configuration: they only rerank BM25's top 25 candidates, so once a typo keeps BM25 from retrieving the target, no reranker can see it. The drop at top 20 is also generally larger than at rank 1, which means typos do damage beyond the very top of the ranking.

Limitations as I see them

First, the queries are not written by real users. Every candidate is generated by Qwen2.5-0.5B under strict constraints and then selected by user profile. Real users may vary more, for example by dropping core terms or adding irrelevant details, and PQB forbids both.

Flip rates are computed only over pairs where at least one query hits, so the denominator differs by setup and cross-setup comparisons need care.

  1. Find different queries in your production logs that led to clicks on the same product, group them by sentence form and whether they contain typos, and compute a similar flip rate to see how sensitive your live system is.

  3. When comparing retrieval designs, report a stability metric alongside average hit rate, such as result agreement across different phrasings of the same need.
  4. PQB's code and data are public, so you can run an offline evaluation on its three categories directly.

papers.title: MICE to Meet You: From Re-ranking Only to End-to-End Retrieval
papers.authors: Victor Morand, Yuxuan Zong, Mathias Vast, Josiane Mothe, Benjamin Piwowarski
papers.abstract: Late-interaction models offer state-of-the-art efficiency-effectiveness trade-offs for neural retrieval by enabling document representations to be pre-computed and efficiently indexed. Yet, their relatively simple interaction mechanisms, typically MaxSim, can limit their effectiveness compared to cross-encoders. MICE, a recently introduced re-ranking architecture, aims to combine cross-encoder-like effectiveness through expressive transformer-based scoring with reduced inference-time computation through document-side pre-computation. However, no practical way to store these document representations was explored. We address this limitation here and introduce MICE-P, the first end-to-end retrieval pipeline with MICE, based on PLAID to index the contextualized document token representations. We conduct a controlled comparison of MICE, ColBERT and cross-encoders by training comparable models using the Ettin Family under matched experimental conditions. Our results show that MICE-P defines a new class of retrieval architecture with an efficiency-effectiveness trade-off of its own: it matches late-interaction retrieval throughput while retaining the effectiveness of cross-encoders.
papers.summary: Cross-encoders rerank candidate documents most accurately, but every candidate must be fully processed for every query. This paper gives the faster MICE architecture a document storage scheme, MICE-P, which comes close to cross-encoder ranking quality at about a quarter of the per-query time. In MICE, the first layers encode the query and the document separately, so the document part can be precomputed; the later layers let query tokens attend to the stored document token representations. MICE-P compresses each document token vector to 128 dimensions, ==stores it in PLAID format, and decompresses it at query time==. PLAID clusters token vectors into centroids and stores each vector as its nearest centroid's ID plus a quantized residual. On BEIR public datasets, its average nDCG@10 is only 0.9 points below a cross-encoder of similar size.

deep_reading.title: MICE to Meet You: From Re-ranking Only to End-to-End Retrieval
deep_reading.content:
Retrieval systems commonly score candidate documents with one of two kinds of model. A cross-encoder reads the query and document together, which is the most accurate but means every candidate must be fully processed for every query. "Late-interaction" models such as ColBERT encode documents token by token ahead of time and store them, so at query time they only run a simple similarity comparison, which is fast but less accurate. MICE (a "cross-encoder with precomputable documents") is a reranking architecture between the two that can precompute document representations, but the original paper left open how to store them. This paper supplies a storage scheme, MICE-P: compress each document token vector to 128 dimensions, store it in the compressed format of PLAID (a multi-vector compressed index commonly used with ColBERT), and decompress it at query time for scoring. ==On 13 public retrieval datasets, the 130-million-parameter MICE-P scores only 0.9 points below a cross-encoder of similar size on average ranking quality at about a quarter of the per-query time, and 0.9 points above the PLAID version of LateOn at about 3 times its latency==.

My take: this is a short engineering paper. Its value is in turning MICE, which could "in theory" precompute documents, into a retrieval pipeline that actually runs, and in comparing it fairly with cross-encoders and ColBERT on the same training data and backbone. It gives teams looking for a middle point between cross-encoders and ColBERT a new option. The costs are also clear. The index is about twice the size of LateOn's, a separate SPLADE retrieval index must be maintained, and on another benchmark, LoTTE, it does not beat LateOn.

## What problem is it actually solving?

Start with how the two mainstream scoring approaches differ. A cross-encoder feeds the query and document into the model as one text, so query and document tokens can see each other in every layer, which makes it the most accurate. But the document representation depends on the query and cannot be computed in advance, so every query requires a full model pass for every candidate.

ColBERT does the opposite and encodes documents and queries separately. Each document token vector can be computed offline and stored in an index. At query time only the query is encoded, and for each query token the model finds the most similar document token and sums these similarities, a step called MaxSim. It is fast, but query and document meet only in a single simple comparison at the end, so it is usually less effective than a cross-encoder.

MICE tries to get the best of both. It splits the model into two parts. The first layers are "contextualization layers" where the query and document are encoded separately, so the document side can be precomputed. The last layers are "interaction layers" where query tokens use attention over the frozen document token representations, capturing richer matching signals than MaxSim. The original paper validated it only for reranking and analyzed efficiency only in theory, without a way to store and search these token representations over a whole collection.

## Method: giving MICE a PLAID store

PLAID is the index commonly used with ColBERT. It first clusters all token vectors with k-means, stores each vector as "the nearest centroid ID plus the residual from that centroid", and quantizes the residual to a few bits, which greatly compresses storage.

MICE-P makes three changes. First, a "bottleneck layer" after the contextualization layers linearly projects each document token vector from the model dimension down to 128 dimensions and then normalizes it, because the PLAID implementation requires normalized vectors. Second, the compressed vectors are stored in PLAID's residual format. At query time, candidate document vectors are decompressed from the store, projected back to the original dimension by a linear layer, and passed to the interaction layers for scoring. Third, MICE-P does not use PLAID's built-in retrieval, because that is tied to MaxSim scoring. Candidates are still retrieved by a separate SPLADE model, which returns the top 100.

The number of quantization bits is a key parameter. The authors measured, on five datasets, how much ranking quality drops at different bit widths relative to no compression.

![Figure 1: the x-axis is the number of residual quantization bits and the y-axis is the change in ranking quality relative to no compression. LateOn is almost unaffected down to 2 bits, while MICE-P drops noticeably at 2 bits and is close to its 8-bit level at 4 bits.](figs/2610.31932/ecir_nbits_ablation.png)

LateOn loses almost nothing at 2 bits. MICE-P drops by more than 0.03 on average at 2 bits (on a scale where 1 is perfect) and by about 0.05 on FiQA and ArguAna, so the authors chose 4 bits. This means MICE-P needs twice the residual storage per vector. My guess is that MICE-P's interaction layers attend closely to every document token vector and are more sensitive to precision, whereas ColBERT only takes the single most similar token, so a coarser approximation matters less.

## Training: converting an existing cross-encoder

The original MICE was distilled directly from a pretrained encoder. This paper takes a different route and converts an already trained Ettin cross-encoder in two steps. In step one, the cross-encoder weights are put into the MICE architecture and training continues on the ranking task, so the model adapts to the new structure in which query and document cannot see each other in the early layers. In step two, the bottleneck is added and only the bottleneck and interaction layers are trained, with the contextualization layers frozen, because the authors found that gradients flowing through the fresh bottleneck damaged those layers.

The training data is 143 million query-passage pairs, each scored by a larger cross-encoder, and the student model fits these scores with a mean squared error loss. For fairness, the authors trained their own ColBERT models on the same data with the same Ettin backbone. Their reproduced Ettin cross-encoder averages 58.0 on the 13 datasets, essentially matching the released checkpoint's 58.1, which shows the training pipeline is sound.

## Results: a new spot between speed and quality

The main evaluation uses BEIR13, the 13 datasets from the BEIR benchmark with training-data overlap removed. So that all designs are measured on the same scale, the metric is nDCG@10, the ranking quality of the top 10 results, multiplied by 100 in the table below. Latency is measured on DBPedia-Entity, with 1 million documents and 349 queries, averaged over five runs. The latencies in the table are approximate values read from Figure 2 of the paper. The other benchmark, LoTTE, is built from forum questions and answers and is commonly used to evaluate ColBERT-style models; it serves here as an out-of-domain check.

| Design | Parameters | BEIR13 average | LoTTE average | Latency per query |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Ettin cross-encoder (reranking SPLADE results) | 150M | 58.8 | 59.1 | about 830 ms |
| MICE-P without PLAID storage | 130M | 58.5 | 58.5 | about 545 ms |
| MICE-P with PLAID storage | 130M | 57.9 | 57.4 | about 200 ms |
| LateOn (ColBERT-style, PLAID retrieval) | 149M | 57.0 | 58.2 | about 60 ms |
| LateOn (reranking SPLADE results) | 149M | 58.6 | 61.3 | about 860 ms |

The table shows that with PLAID storage, MICE-P loses only 0.6 points on BEIR13 relative to the uncompressed version, while latency falls from about 545 ms to about 200 ms. Compared with the cross-encoder, it gives up 0.9 points and is about 4 times faster. Compared with the PLAID version of LateOn, it is 0.9 points better but about 3 times slower. On the paper's quality-versus-latency plot, it fills the empty region between LateOn and the cross-encoder. The authors also report that, without compression, MICE needs about 60% of the compute of the corresponding cross-encoder.

![Figure 2, left: the x-axis is latency per query and the y-axis is the BEIR13 average. Hollow markers use PLAID storage and filled markers do not. The box on the left marks MICE-P with PLAID storage, at about 200 ms and scoring above the ColBERT-style models nearby.](figs/2610.31932/pareto_ecir.png)

There is also a side finding. The authors' own ColBERT models do well when reranking SPLADE results, but they drop sharply when PLAID does the retrieval itself; the 150M version falls from 57.4 to 47.3. The official LateOn drops far less. The authors suspect that their ColBERT models used a loss that only fits scores, without contrastive learning and hard negatives, so the token vectors are not spread out enough and PLAID's cluster-based retrieval breaks down.

## Limitations as I see them

First, storage doubles. On Climate-FEVER with 5 million documents, MICE-P's total index is 100.1 GB, of which the PLAID store is 90.2 GB and the SPLADE index 9.9 GB, while LateOn needs 51.8 GB. The main reason is that MICE-P needs 4-bit rather than 2-bit quantization.

Second, the advantage is not consistent. On LoTTE, MICE-P with PLAID storage scores 57.4, below PLAID-based LateOn at 58.2 and reranking LateOn at 61.3. So the claim of being more accurate than ColBERT currently holds only on BEIR13.

Third, it is not yet truly end-to-end retrieval. Candidate retrieval still relies on a separate SPLADE model, so the system has two indexes to maintain. The authors list retrieving directly with PLAID as future work.

## How a team could try this

1. If you rerank with a cross-encoder in production and latency is tight, evaluate MICE-P as a replacement: take the top 100 from SPLADE or another retriever and compare latency and ranking quality.
2. Test quantization bit widths on your own data first; the paper shows MICE-P is sensitive at 2 bits and steadier at 4 bits.
3. Evaluate on two kinds of datasets so you do not win on only one benchmark.
4. The authors released code, configurations and all models, so you can convert an Ettin cross-encoder with the two-step training recipe directly.

## One-sentence conclusion

==MICE-P makes a "cross-encoder with precomputable documents" actually run, reaching near cross-encoder quality on BEIR13 at about a quarter of the time, at the cost of an index roughly twice as large plus an extra retrieval index.==

| Dimension | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Importance | Medium. The quality-speed trade-off is a long-standing problem in retrieval systems |
| Novelty | Medium-low. Mainly combines the existing MICE and PLAID, plus training techniques |
| Evidence | Medium. Fair comparison on the same backbone and data, but latency is measured on one dataset and it does not lead on LoTTE |
| Engineering cost | Medium. Requires maintaining both SPLADE and PLAID indexes, with about twice ColBERT's storage |
| Worth trying | Yes, for teams whose cross-encoder latency is too high |

papers.title: Collection-Date Assignment Redirects Answers in Temporal QA
papers.authors: Minsu Oh, Seunghui Jwa, Soo Kyun Kim, Yeo-Chan Yoon
papers.abstract: A collection date records when a source revision was acquired, not when its contents changed. Can assigning this metadata redirect temporal question answering despite unchanged evidence? Swapping the question day and following day between two revisions lowers later-reference exact match (EM) by 37.6-51.4 percentage points across five open-weight LLMs on 595 Wikipedia pages, replicated on 128 disjoint pages. Previous-day swaps retain 29.0-39.6-point losses on 497 pages. Seven prompt variants, including explicit ignore-collection instructions and archived-revision provenance, retain the effect. Fictional answers and English month-name question dates show that remembered answers and identical date strings are unnecessary. Matched thinking reduces Qwen3.5's penalty from 30.1 to 11.1 points, while native reasoners vary. Two API LLMs show small Wikipedia swap effects and rarely shift to earlier answers on fictional records. Large swap-induced losses concentrate around the question date; swaps between distant dates have much smaller effects. Adding fields containing one observed acquisition date lowers EM relative to omission in three of five LLMs after correction. The diagnostic isolates metadata effects from changing evidence or missing the relevant revision, and provides a practical audit for temporal QA inputs.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented question-answering systems often attach a collection date to web snippets, and this paper finds that ==this field, which only records the fetch day, can steer an LLM's answer the wrong way==, even though it says nothing about when the content changed. Ask which team an ice hockey player played for on a given day, and put both an older and a newer Wikipedia revision in the context. The texts and revision timestamps stay fixed; only the collection dates are swapped, so the older revision's date equals the question date. The experiment covers 595 Wikipedia pages. The swap lowers five open-weight models' exact-match rate on the newer answer by 37.6 to 51.4 percentage points, and telling the model not to choose by collection time barely reduces the loss.

deep_reading.title: Collection-Date Assignment Redirects Answers in Temporal QA
deep_reading.content:
Retrieval-augmented question-answering systems often attach a "collection date" to retrieved web snippets, meaning the day the content was fetched, not the day it was last changed. This paper finds that this field can steer a large language model's answer the wrong way. Suppose the question is "Which team did a certain ice hockey player play for on July 16, 2025?" and the context holds both an older Wikipedia revision (listing his old team) and a newer one (listing his new team). The texts and revision timestamps of both stay fixed, and only the collection dates are swapped: the older revision gets a collection date exactly equal to the question date, and the newer one gets the following day. ==On 595 Wikipedia pages, this swap lowers the exact-match rate for the newer answer by 37.6 to 51.4 percentage points across five open-weight language models; explicitly telling the model "do not choose answers by collection time" still leaves losses of 37.9 to 50.8 points==.

My take: teams building retrieval-augmented question answering, especially those that place several versions or several sources in the same context, should read this. It shows that metadata is not harmless extra information. The limitation is that the paper cannot say how often "collection date exactly equals question date" happens in real systems. The two commercial API models are barely affected, so the conclusion applies mainly to open-weight models.

## What problem is it actually solving?

Temporal question answering involves three different times. The question date is the moment the question asks about, such as "which team on July 16, 2025". The revision timestamp is when a version's content was written. The collection date is when the system fetched that version. Fetching an old version does not make its content newer, so in principle the collection date should not affect which version matches the question date.

In practice such metadata is common. Some web-scraping tools return a fetch-time field with their results, and retrieval systems may put cache times into the prompt as well. The paper asks: once both versions are already in the context, can changing only the collection dates make the model choose the wrong answer?

## How the experiment is set up

The data is 595 Wikipedia pages, each with two revisions in which a recorded fact changed, such as an athlete moving to a new team. The later question date falls after the newer revision, so the correct answer is the content of the newer revision. Each input contains the question, the texts and revision timestamps of both versions, and a collection-date field.

The core manipulation is the "question-date swap". In one assignment, the newer revision's collection date equals the question date and the older revision's is one day later. In the other, it is the reverse. Both assignments use the same pair of dates, the texts, timestamps and question stay fixed, and both orderings of the two versions are tested and averaged. The metric is exact match, the share of answers that, after normalization, are identical to the reference answer.

The authors also repeat the main experiment on 128 non-overlapping pages and use those pages to test reasoning modes and two commercial API models.

When the older revision gets the question date, all five models answer the newer fact far less often, and the share answering with the older fact rises in step.

| Model | Newer revision gets question date | Older revision gets question date | Drop |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen2.5-7B | 68.4% | 28.3% | 40.1 points |
| Phi-4 | 51.0% | 3.7% | 47.3 points |
| Mistral-24B | 73.7% | 22.3% | 51.4 points |
| Qwen3.5-35B | 71.4% | 33.8% | 37.6 points |
| Qwen2.5-72B | 77.1% | 28.3% | 48.7 points |

Each cell is the exact-match rate for the newer answer. Comparing the "older 0, newer 1" cell with the "older 1, newer 0" cell gives the question-date swap, and the former is clearly lower.](figs/2610.32191/w2_factorial.png)

## Ruling out other explanations

The authors use a series of controls to check whether something else causes this.

First, do models simply prefer the version collected earlier? On 497 pages, the authors set the other date to the day before the question date, so the version that gets the question date is now the one collected later. The drop is still 29.0 to 39.6 points, so it is not just a preference for earlier collection.

Second, is the prompt ambiguous? On 128 pages the authors tried seven prompt variants, including an explicit instruction not to choose by collection time, a statement that the snippets are archived revisions of the same page, a renamed field, and moving the field below the text. The loss remains under every variant, at least about 36 points.

Third, do models answer from memory, or is it just identical strings? Repeating the test on 128 records about fictional entities (for example, a made-up company moving its headquarters from city A to city B) produces drops of 92.2 to 95.7 points, so the model does not need to know the answer beforehand. Writing the question date with English month names, so it no longer matches the numeric format of the collection date, still leaves losses of 31.6 to 53.1 points.

Fourth, distant dates have almost no effect. When both collection dates fall months after the question and differ by only seven days, swapping them changes results by just 0 to 6.2 points. So what matters is a collection date that equals or sits close to the question date.

## Reasoning modes and commercial models

With thinking mode on, Qwen3.5-35B's loss from the swap falls from 30.1 to 11.1 points. Both random seeds show the reduction, but the loss does not disappear. Other models with built-in reasoning vary widely: Ministral-3-14B loses 13.1 points and Nemotron-3-Nano loses 51.8, so "turn on reasoning and it is solved" does not hold.

## Limitations as I see them

First, the setting is constructed. The paper deliberately sets collection dates equal to or right next to the question date, and how often such a coincidence happens in real systems is unclear. The authors also tested real fetch dates (six months to two years after the question date): showing that field lowered exact match by 3.5 to 15.2 points compared with not showing it, much smaller than in the swap experiment.

Second, the main experiment covers only single factual changes on Wikipedia, such as teams or positions. In more complex multi-document reasoning, the effect of metadata may differ.

Third, the conclusion applies mainly to open-weight models. The two commercial API models are barely affected, and why they are robust remains an open question.

## How a team could try this

1. Check whether your retrieval-augmented prompts include fields such as fetch time, cache time or publication date, and confirm whether the model really needs each one.
2. Run an audit the way the paper does: keep texts and revision timestamps fixed, swap the date fields of two versions, and see whether the answer changes.
3. If your system knows each version's identity, pick the latest valid version by revision time before generation instead of handing several versions to the model to choose from.
4. Do not expect an instruction to "ignore this field" in the prompt to remove the effect; the paper shows it barely helps.

==Seemingly harmless metadata such as collection dates noticeably changes open-weight models' answers in temporal question answering, and asking them to ignore it does not help; the safest approach is to choose the version before generation or not show the model irrelevant dates at all.==

|---|---|
| Importance | Medium-high. Retrieval-augmented systems commonly attach all kinds of date metadata |
| Novelty | Medium. The core is one clean controlled experiment with careful controls |
| Evidence | Strong. Five open-weight models, two disjoint page sets, seven prompts, fictional-entity and format controls |
| Engineering cost | Low. The audit method is simple and can be applied directly to your own system |
| Worth trying | Yes, use its swap method to audit your own prompt templates |

papers.title: From Noisy Retrieval to Decision Evidence: Silver Evidence Demonstrations for In-Context Learning
papers.authors: Masoud Monajatipoor, Fazlolah Mohaghegh, Hamid Reza Hassanzadeh, Akash Uttamrao Bhoite, Robert E. Tillman
papers.abstract: RAG and retrieval-augmented few-shot ICL can struggle when decision-relevant evidence is buried in long, noisy context. Retrieved passages and demonstrations may contain redundant or distracting information. Although expert-labeled development examples may identify the text supporting each decision, these annotations are typically used only as answer-side rationales rather than as supervision for filtering noisy retrieval. We propose silver-evidence demonstrations, which replace raw retrieved passages in ICL examples with generated, target-conditioned evidence summaries. For each labeled development example, an LLM generates silver evidence without access to the expert label or gold evidence; this evidence is then paired with the expert label and gold evidence where available. At test time, a single structured call generates silver evidence from retrieved passages and then predicts the final label and decision evidence. Across EI 2.0, SciFact, synthetic policy retrieval, and HICRIC/IMR data, our full method improves over equally sized gold-only ICL (label-only for policy) on three of four datasets and improves evidence F1 on all annotated datasets. It also achieves higher mean label accuracy than InstructRAG-style ICL on all four datasets. These results suggest that replacing demonstration-side retrieved passages with compact, target-conditioned silver evidence is particularly useful for decisions based on long and noisy text, where it reduces distracting context while preserving decision-relevant signals and expert supervision.
papers.summary: In retrieval-augmented few-shot decisions, such as making a call against a pile of policy documents, the key evidence is often buried in long, noisy retrieved passages, and the raw passages in the demonstrations add even more distraction. This paper ==replaces the raw retrieved passages in each demonstration with a compact evidence summary that an LLM writes for that decision==, without seeing the expert answer, and then pairs it with the expert label and evidence. At test time a single call first writes the evidence summary, then gives the decision and its support. On a synthetic policy retrieval task, accuracy is 33.0 points higher than expert-only demonstrations of the same count, and 8.0 points higher on SciFact scientific claim verification.

papers.title: The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering
papers.authors: Debopriyo Banerjee, Owais Aijaz, Ahmer Tabassum, Zhuohan Xie, Preslav Nakov, Veselin Stoyanov
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document-level context that resolves cross-passage references. We introduce evidence-based generation (EBG), requiring models to return an answer with line-level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric that scores correctness and grounding simultaneously. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks—MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP, a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER with realistic short paper cues—and pair them with a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K–1M characters. Across eight frontier proprietary and three open-weight LLMs, EBG isolates two RAG limitations that long-context models avoid: similarity retrieval surfaces any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and chunking destroys document meta-information needed to resolve identity-bearing queries. EBG also exposes grounding failures invisible to answer-only evaluation, including incomplete citations in two-needle settings and a widening gap between Ans and Ans+Evid when context contradicts parametric knowledge. Data and code are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/LC-EBG.
papers.summary: When retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fails on long-document questions, is retrieval missing evidence or is the model misreading it? This paper asks models to return line-level citations with each answer and checks both whether the answer is right and whether the cited lines support it. Across 8 frontier proprietary and 3 open-weight models, the bottleneck is mainly retrieval: ==similarity search easily finds one relevant passage but rarely finds every passage a multi-fact question needs==. Chunking also discards document-level information, such as which paper a passage came from, so questions that depend on the source go wrong. Giving the whole material to a long-context model avoids both problems.

papers.title: Before the Ticket: Grounding HPC User Support in Documentation and Resolved Tickets with an Agentic LLM Assistant
papers.authors: Elham J. Barezi, Primus C Kabuo, Niveditha Nerella
papers.abstract: Most questions that reach an HPC help desk have already been answered in the center's user guides or in a ticket someone else filed last semester; users still file new tickets because the guides are hard to navigate and the ticket history is not theirs to search. We present an assistant that answers from both sources: an orchestrator calls two tools over the Model Context Protocol, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the live documentation and a Llama-3-8B model fine-tuned with QLoRA on 11,244 query-resolution pairs mined from historical tickets, and merges their answers. Every model runs on-premises or on the university's hosted LLM service because ticket data may not leave the institution. On 400 held-out tickets from Purdue's Rosen Center for Advanced Computing, disjoint from training and free of near-duplicates, and evaluated by two judges from model families that generated none of the answers, fine-tuning on resolutions rewritten into self-service guidance is the clear winner in agreement with RCAC's resolutions (BERTScore F1 improves from 0.06 to 0.27 over the base model) and is judged most correct on average. The end-to-end system does not improve on its tools, although they are complementary: choosing the better answer per question would exceed either tool (judged correctness 3.41 versus 3.20, an oracle bound), while the merge follows the documentation tool in 78% of answers. Returning one tool's answer instead recovers the fine-tuned tool's quality (3.19 versus 2.66), but neither a learned selector nor an LLM verifier beats that tool alone.
papers.summary: Most questions reaching a supercomputing center's help desk were already answered in the user guides or in someone else's old ticket, but the guides are hard to navigate and users cannot search other people's tickets. This Purdue paper builds an assistant: one tool runs retrieval-augmented generation over the live documentation, another is a Llama-3-8B fine-tuned on historical ticket questions and resolutions, and a final step combines the two answers into one, with source links. On 400 held-out tickets, ==fine-tuning on resolutions rewritten as self-service guides works best==. The merged system, however, does not beat either tool alone, and its merged answer follows the documentation tool 78% of the time.

papers.title: GeoLEON-CLIP: Graph-Anchored Multimodal Contrastive Learning for Geographic Region Representation
papers.authors: Radoslaw Malek, Szymon Soltysiak, Aleksandra Kawala-Sterniuk, Piotr Szymanski
papers.abstract: Geographic regions are multimodal: satellite imagery captures visual morphology, text conveys human-interpretable semantics, and map structures describe urban context. Existing geospatial contrastive methods typically align image-text or image-location pairs, underusing structured map data. We introduce GeoLEON-CLIP, a graph-anchored contrastive framework that aligns three views of each H3-indexed region: an OpenStreetMap-derived graph embedding, a satellite image crop, and a textual description. Frozen pretrained LEON graph embeddings provide a semantic anchor between vision and language. Frozen graph, image, and text encoders are connected by trainable residual projection heads and trained with a symmetric tri-modal contrastive objective. Experiments show strong graph-image and graph-text alignment; graph-image retrieval achieves the best cross-modal performance in a mixed-resolution pool. To evaluate the anchoring hypothesis, we propose chained cross-modal recall $\mathrm{R}@A@B$, which routes retrieval through the graph modality and compares it with direct retrieval under a matched candidate budget. At $\mathrm{R}@1@1$, image$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$text and text$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$image outperform direct image-text retrieval by 4.8 and 4.4 points, respectively, despite using a single intermediate cell. Downstream probes show task-dependent gains, with the largest improvements on Airbnb and Beijing housing. These results indicate that OpenStreetMap graph structure can anchor multimodal representations combining maps, imagery, and language.
papers.summary: A city area can be described by satellite imagery, by text, or by the road and amenity structure in OpenStreetMap, yet most existing methods align only images and text. This paper proposes GeoLEON-CLIP, which aligns all three views of each grid cell in one vector space and ==trains both satellite images and text to align with the same cell's map-structure embedding, which anchors images to text==. All three encoders stay frozen and only projection heads are trained. Retrieving the best-matching map cell from an image, then using that cell's map embedding to find text, beats direct image-to-text retrieval on top-1 hit rate by 4.8 points, and the reverse direction gains 4.4 points. In downstream prediction, Beijing housing prices and Airbnb data improve the most.

papers.title: Synthetic-to-Real Text-Based Person Anomaly Search via Multi-Model Retrieval Fusion and Cross-Encoder Reranking
papers.authors: Eugene Denteh, Blessing Agyei Kyem, Andrews Danyo, Joshua Kofi Asamoah, Richard Dzinyela, Solomon Owusu-Ansah, Dickson G. Asiedu, Armstrong Aboah
papers.abstract: Text-based person anomaly search requires a model to retrieve individuals from a large image gallery using natural-language descriptions of both appearance and behavior. This task is challenging because model training relies on synthetic image-text pairs, whereas evaluation is performed on real surveillance images containing domain differences, near-duplicate frames, and many visually similar distractors. We present a multi-model retrieval and reranking framework designed to improve synthetic-to-real transfer. The framework first adapts Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B to synthetic person descriptions using bidirectional contrastive learning, explicit negative sampling, false-negative masking, and domain randomization. It then combines the normalized scores of six complementary Qwen3-VL checkpoints with those of a frozen SigLIP2 model using four-view gallery encoding. The fused retrieval scores identify the strongest candidates, which are jointly evaluated with the query using Qwen3-VL-Reranker-8B. The cross-encoder and retrieval scores are subsequently blended to produce the final ranking. We also construct a distractor-matched validation protocol entirely from synthetic data to select checkpoint weights, fusion coefficients, candidate depths, and reranking parameters without accessing the official test images. The final system achieves 94.7815% mAP and 90.8493% R@1 under the official AI City Challenge 2026 Track 4 test setting, with a reported eighth-place finish on the public leaderboard.
papers.summary: Finding a person in surveillance footage from one sentence means describing both appearance and abnormal behavior. The hard part is that training can use only synthetic image-text pairs, while testing uses real surveillance frames full of near-duplicate neighboring frames and look-alike distractors. This paper fine-tunes a Qwen3-VL embedding model on synthetic descriptions, retrieves by a weighted sum of several models' normalized similarity scores, and reranks the top candidates with a cross-encoder. ==Every setting is chosen on a validation set built only from synthetic data, without touching the official test images==. The system reaches 94.78% mAP on the AI City Challenge text-based person anomaly search track, placing 8th on the public leaderboard.
